front: Type 2 diabetes with established ASCVD, heart failure or CKD: which drug classes regardless of A1C, and the usual A1C goal?
bottom: Add organ-protective agents irrespective of A1C.

bullets.clue: ASCVD: GLP-1 RA and/or SGLT2i; HF: SGLT2i; CKD: SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA.
bullets.treat: Lifestyle plus drug therapy; A1C goal often <7%.
bullets.trap: Don't wait for A1C to rise first.

back: Add organ-protective agents irrespective of A1C. Key clue: ASCVD: GLP-1 RA and/or SGLT2i; HF: SGLT2i; CKD: SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA. First-line: Lifestyle plus drug therapy; A1C goal often <7%. Exam trap: Don't wait for A1C to rise first.

diagram.alt: Type 2 diabetes: GLP-1 RA or SGLT2 inhibitor for ASCVD, SGLT2 inhibitor for heart failure, either for CKD, regardless of A1C.

source.guideline: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, sections 6 and 9
source.recommendation: ADA 2026 9.7: ASCVD/high risk include GLP-1 RA and/or SGLT2i irrespective of A1C (A). 9.8: HF SGLT2i (A). 9.10: CKD eGFR 20–60 and/or albuminuria SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA (A). 9.6 consider initial combination. Section 6: A1C <7% appropriate for many, individualized.

front: Insulin-treated patient found confused with glucose 45 mg/dL: hypoglycemia level, treatment, and what to prescribe?

bullets.treat: Alert: 15–20 g glucose, recheck in 15 min; unable to swallow: glucagon.
bullets.trap: Everyone on insulin needs glucagon prescribed.

back: Level 2 hypoglycemia (<54 mg/dL). Key clue: Level 3: altered status needing assistance. First-line: Alert: 15–20 g glucose, recheck in 15 min; unable to swallow: glucagon. Exam trap: Everyone on insulin needs glucagon prescribed.

diagram.alt: Hypoglycemia levels: level 1 below 70, level 2 below 54, level 3 severe needing assistance; glucose 15 to 20 grams or glucagon.

source.guideline: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, section 6
source.recommendation: ADA 2026: level 2 <54 mg/dL; level 3 severe event with altered status requiring assistance; glucose 15–20 g preferred for conscious patient, recheck 15 min; glucagon prescribed for those on insulin or at high risk.

front: Free T4 is low and TSH is high. Which gland failed, and how is hormone replaced?
bottom: The thyroid failed. Pituitary TSH rises because the feedback signal is gone.

bullets.clue: A low TSH with a low free T4 is central, not primary, hypothyroidism.
bullets.treat: Levothyroxine on an empty stomach. Recheck TSH in about 6 weeks. Start lower in older adults and in coronary disease.
bullets.trap: Biotin can make free T4 look high and TSH look low.

back: The thyroid failed. Pituitary TSH rises because the feedback signal is gone. Key clue: A low TSH with a low free T4 is central, not primary, hypothyroidism. First-line: Levothyroxine on an empty stomach. Recheck TSH in about 6 weeks. Start lower in older adults and in coronary disease. Exam trap: Biotin can make free T4 look high and TSH look low.

diagram.alt: The thyroid failed. Pituitary TSH rises because the feedback signal is gone.

source.guideline: ATA Guidelines for the Treatment of Hypothyroidism (2014, still current as of 2026)
source.recommendation: ATA: levothyroxine; titrate to normal TSH; recheck TSH 4–6 weeks after dose change; take 60 min before breakfast or at bedtime, separate from calcium/iron; avoid TSH <0.1 especially older/postmenopausal.

front: Fever, tachycardia, agitation and known Graves disease: diagnosis and treatment sequence?
bottom: Thyroid storm: multimodal therapy in ICU.

bullets.treat: Beta-blocker, PTU, then iodine, plus steroids.

back: Thyroid storm: multimodal therapy in ICU. Key clue: Burch-Wartofsky score ≥45 supports storm. First-line: Beta-blocker, PTU, then iodine, plus steroids. Exam trap: Give thionamide before iodine.

diagram.alt: Thyroid storm: beta-blocker, propylthiouracil, then iodine, steroids and ICU care.

source.guideline: ATA Guidelines for Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis (2016) (still current as of 2026)
source.recommendation: ATA 2016: TSH initial test; beta-blockade for symptomatic thyrotoxicosis; BWPS ≥45 with systemic decompensation warrants aggressive multimodal therapy: beta-blocker, antithyroid drug, inorganic iodide, corticosteroid, supportive ICU care.

front: Thyroid nodule found on exam: first test and when to scan versus biopsy?

bullets.clue: Low TSH: radionuclide scan; hot nodule rarely malignant.
bullets.treat: Normal or high TSH: ultrasound, FNA by size and sonographic pattern.

back: Check TSH first. Key clue: Low TSH: radionuclide scan; hot nodule rarely malignant. First-line: Normal or high TSH: ultrasound, FNA by size and sonographic pattern. Exam trap: Don't biopsy a hyperfunctioning (hot) nodule.

diagram.alt: Thyroid nodule: TSH first; low TSH leads to scan, normal TSH to ultrasound and FNA by pattern.

source.guideline: ATA Management Guidelines for Adult Patients with Thyroid Nodules (2025; split from DTC guideline)
source.recommendation: ATA nodule recs 2A–C: measure TSH; if subnormal, radionuclide (preferably 123I) scan; if normal or high, no scan as initial imaging. Rec 6: ultrasound with neck node survey for all; rec 7: FNA procedure of choice, by size and sonographic pattern; purely cystic nodules need no FNA.

front: Hypotension, hyperkalemia, hyperpigmentation: diagnosis and treatment; and first screening tests for Cushing?
bottom: Primary adrenal insufficiency: glucocorticoid plus mineralocorticoid.

bullets.clue: Low morning cortisol, high ACTH; confirm with cosyntropin.
bullets.treat: Hydrocortisone 15–25 mg/day in 2–3 doses; fludrocortisone 50–100 µg.
bullets.trap: Cushing screen: UFC, late-night salivary cortisol or 1 mg DST.

back: Primary adrenal insufficiency: glucocorticoid plus mineralocorticoid. Key clue: Low morning cortisol, high ACTH; confirm with cosyntropin. First-line: Hydrocortisone 15–25 mg/day in 2–3 doses; fludrocortisone 50–100 µg. Exam trap: Cushing screen: UFC, late-night salivary cortisol or 1 mg DST.

diagram.alt: Adrenal insufficiency: high ACTH, low cortisol; hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. Cushing screening uses urine free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol or dexamethasone suppression.

source.guideline: Endocrine Society: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (2016); Diagnosis of Cushing Syndrome (2008) (still current as of 2026)
source.recommendation: ES 2008: screen Cushing with one high-accuracy test (24-h UFC, late-night salivary cortisol, 1 mg overnight DST); abnormal → second test. ES 2016 3.2: hydrocortisone 15–25 mg (or cortisone acetate 20–35 mg) in 2–3 divided doses, highest at awakening; 3.7: fludrocortisone 50–100 µg start, no salt restriction.

front: Hypertension: who gets screened for primary aldosteronism, and how is pheochromocytoma tested?
bottom: Screen all with hypertension for primary aldosteronism.

bullets.treat: Positive ARR: confirm, then imaging and adrenal vein sampling.
bullets.trap: Pheo: plasma free or urine fractionated metanephrines first.

back: Screen all with hypertension for primary aldosteronism. Key clue: Aldosterone-to-renin ratio with potassium. First-line: Positive ARR: confirm, then imaging and adrenal vein sampling. Exam trap: Pheo: plasma free or urine fractionated metanephrines first.

diagram.alt: Primary aldosteronism screening with aldosterone and renin in hypertension; pheochromocytoma tested with metanephrines.

source.guideline: Endocrine Society: Primary Aldosteronism (2025); Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma (2014)
source.recommendation: ES 2025: suggest screening all hypertensive patients with aldosterone and renin (ARR) plus potassium; positive → confirmation/further evaluation. ES 2014: initial testing plasma free or urine fractionated metanephrines; supine sampling for plasma.

front: Incidental calcium 11.8 with high PTH in a 45-year-old: diagnosis and who needs surgery?
bottom: Primary hyperparathyroidism; surgery if any criterion met.

bullets.clue: Calcium >1 above normal, age <50, eGFR <60, T-score ≤−2.5, stones.
bullets.trap: Age under 50 alone qualifies for surgery.

back: Primary hyperparathyroidism; surgery if any criterion met. Key clue: Calcium >1 above normal, age <50, eGFR <60, T-score ≤−2.5, stones. First-line: Parathyroidectomy is definitive. Exam trap: Age under 50 alone qualifies for surgery.

diagram.alt: Primary hyperparathyroidism: high calcium and PTH; surgery for calcium more than 1 above normal, age under 50, kidney or bone criteria.

source.guideline: Fifth International Workshop on Primary Hyperparathyroidism (2022)
source.recommendation: 2022 workshop: surgery if calcium >1 mg/dL above ULN, age <50, eGFR <60, T-score ≤−2.5 or vertebral fracture, nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis, or hypercalciuria.

front: Free T4 is high and TSH is low. What feedback loop explains that, and why can prolactin rise when dopamine falls?
bottom: Thyroid hormone suppresses TSH. Dopamine suppresses prolactin.

bullets.clue: The hypothalamus releases TRH and dopamine.
bullets.treat: High T4 with high TSH is not primary hyperthyroidism. A dopamine agonist treats prolactinoma.
bullets.trap: Primary hypothyroidism can raise prolactin through TRH. Check TSH first.

back: Thyroid hormone suppresses TSH. Dopamine suppresses prolactin. Key clue: The hypothalamus releases TRH and dopamine. First-line: High T4 with high TSH is not primary hyperthyroidism. A dopamine agonist treats prolactinoma. Exam trap: Primary hypothyroidism can raise prolactin through TRH. Check TSH first.

diagram.alt: Thyroid hormone suppresses TSH. Dopamine suppresses prolactin.

source.guideline: 2016 ATA hyperthyroidism guideline; Endocrine Society prolactinoma guideline (2011, still current as of 2026)
source.recommendation: ES 2011: cabergoline preferred dopamine agonist for symptomatic micro/macroprolactinoma. Review: fluid restriction first-line for chronic SIADH; avoid overcorrection.

front: Glucose 900, osmolality 350, no significant ketosis, pH 7.35: diagnosis and first step?

bullets.treat: Aggressive IV fluids first, then insulin.

back: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state. Key clue: Glucose ≥600, effective osmolality >300, BHB <3.0, pH ≥7.3. First-line: Aggressive IV fluids first, then insulin. Exam trap: Potassium <3.5: replace and hold insulin.

diagram.alt: HHS: glucose 600 or higher, effective osmolality above 300, minimal ketosis; fluids first, hold insulin if potassium below 3.5.

source.guideline: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults Consensus Report (2024)
source.recommendation: 2024 consensus: HHS glucose ≥600, effective osmolality >300 (or total >320), BHB <3.0, pH ≥7.3 and HCO3 ≥15. K+ <3.5: replace and delay insulin. Fluids are initial therapy.

front: Months of extreme thirst and very large urine volumes. Glucose is normal. How do you separate the two causes?
bottom: Diabetes insipidus: dilute urine despite high-normal or high sodium.

bullets.clue: Urine osmolality <200 mOsm/kg; desmopressin corrects central, not nephrogenic.
bullets.treat: Central (AVP deficiency): desmopressin. Nephrogenic: thiazide plus NSAID.
bullets.trap: Skip water deprivation if already hypernatremic with dilute urine.

back: Diabetes insipidus: dilute urine despite high-normal or high sodium. Key clue: Urine osmolality <200 mOsm/kg; desmopressin corrects central, not nephrogenic. First-line: Central (AVP deficiency): desmopressin. Nephrogenic: thiazide plus NSAID. Exam trap: Skip water deprivation if already hypernatremic with dilute urine.

diagram.alt: Diabetes insipidus: dilute urine despite high-normal or high sodium.

source.guideline: International expert consensus on congenital nephrogenic DI (AVP resistance), Nat Rev Nephrol 2024; Atila, Refardt, Christ-Crain: AVP deficiency review, Nat Rev Endocrinol 2024; Working Group on renaming diabetes insipidus, JCEM 2022/2023
source.recommendation: Consensus 2024 (congenital NDI): work-up with serum Na, serum osmolality and urine osmolality; urine osmolality <200 mOsm/kg with high-normal or high Na indicates DI; DDAVP test separates central DI from NDI; water deprivation test contraindicated with hypernatremic dehydration and inappropriately dilute urine; thiazide plus prostaglandin synthesis inhibitor started in symptomatic infants and children. Review 2024: hypertonic-saline copeptin has replaced water deprivation as diagnostic gold standard; desmopressin mainstay for AVP deficiency. 2022 statement: central DI renamed AVP deficiency, nephrogenic DI renamed AVP resistance.
